A **microprogrammed** control unit stores the control signals in a small fast memory, the **control memory**, and executes them like a program. Each word of control memory is a **microinstruction** whose bits either *are* the control signals or encode them. The sequence of microinstructions that implements one machine instruction is a **microroutine**, and the whole collection is the **microprogram**, written by the machine's designer and burned into ROM. Adding an instruction means writing more microcode, not rewiring, which is why CISC machines with hundreds of complex instructions are almost always microprogrammed.

Three levels of program are now in play, and they are regularly confused:

| Level | Stored in | Written by | Unit of execution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Program | main memory | programmer | machine instruction |
| Microprogram | control memory | CPU designer | microinstruction |
| Nanoprogram | nanomemory | CPU designer | nanoinstruction |

Control memory is **read-only in normal operation**. Machines with writable control store exist (they allow emulation of other instruction sets), but the default assumption in an exam question is ROM.

## The pieces of a microprogrammed control unit

- **Control memory (CM)** — holds the microprogram. If it has $2^k$ words, addresses are $k$ bits.
- **Control address register (CAR)** — the microprogram counter, $k$ bits wide, holding the address of the microinstruction being executed.
- **Control data register (CDR)**, sometimes called the microinstruction register — holds the microinstruction while its fields are decoded. Not all designs have one; omitting it saves a clock but forces the control memory read to complete within the same period.
- **Subroutine register (SBR)** — saves the return address for microsubroutines. It is usually a single register or a small stack, which limits microprogram subroutine nesting depth.
- **Sequencer / next-address generator** — a multiplexer that decides what CAR gets next.

**Address sequencing** is the interesting part. After a microinstruction, the next control address can come from four places:

1. **CAR + 1** — the default, straight-line microcode.
2. **The address field of the current microinstruction** — an unconditional or conditional microbranch.
3. **The mapping logic** — at the start of executing a machine instruction, the opcode is transformed into the starting address of its microroutine.
4. **SBR** — return from a microsubroutine.

**Mapping** is the mechanism that connects the machine instruction to its microroutine. The simplest scheme takes a 4-bit opcode, prefixes a 0 and appends two 0s, giving the 7-bit control address

$$0\;\;O_3O_2O_1O_0\;\;0\,0$$

so routines start at addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, … and each machine instruction gets **four** words of control memory before the next routine begins. If a routine needs more than four microinstructions it branches out to the free area above address 64. The general rule: with an $n$-bit opcode mapped as $0\,|\,\text{opcode}\,|\,00$, each microroutine is allotted $2^2 = 4$ words and the mapped region occupies $2^{n+2}$ words.

blocks.title: A concrete microinstruction format
blocks.text:
The standard 20-bit microinstruction used in the teaching design:

| Field | Bits | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | 3 | one of 7 microoperations (plus 000 = none) |
| F2 | 3 | one of 7 microoperations |
| F3 | 3 | one of 7 microoperations |
| CD | 2 | condition to test |
| BR | 2 | branch type |
| AD | 7 | branch address |

CD selects the status bit: $00 = U$ (unconditional, always 1), $01 = I$ (indirect bit), $10 = S$ (sign of AC), $11 = Z$ (AC is zero).

BR selects the sequencing action: $00 = $ JMP (if condition, $CAR \leftarrow AD$, else $CAR \leftarrow CAR+1$), $01 = $ CALL (as JMP but also $SBR \leftarrow CAR+1$), $10 = $ RET ($CAR \leftarrow SBR$), $11 = $ MAP ($CAR \leftarrow$ mapped opcode).

This is a **vertical** format: three encoded 3-bit fields select at most three simultaneous microoperations out of 21, rather than giving every signal its own bit.

## Horizontal versus vertical microprogramming

This is the comparison the exam asks about most, and the distinction is about **encoding**, not about physical layout.

**Horizontal microprogramming** gives (nearly) every control signal its own bit in the microinstruction. With $n$ control signals the microinstruction is $n$ bits wide plus sequencing fields.

- Maximum parallelism: any set of compatible microoperations can be issued in one microinstruction.
- No decoding delay, so it is **faster**.
- Very wide microinstructions, so control memory is **large** and mostly zeros.
- Harder to write, because the microprogrammer must know which signals conflict.

**Vertical microprogramming** partitions the control signals into groups of **mutually exclusive** signals and encodes each group into a field, which a decoder expands at run time.

- Microinstruction is **much narrower**, so control memory is small.
- Decoders add a gate delay, so it is **slower**.
- Only one signal per field can be active, so parallelism is limited to the number of fields.
- Microcode looks like ordinary assembly language and is easier to write.

The encoding arithmetic is simple and is what numerical questions test: a group of $m$ mutually exclusive signals needs $\lceil \log_2 (m+1) \rceil$ bits — the $+1$ is the "no operation in this group" code, and forgetting it is the standard mistake.

**Nanoprogramming** is the two-level compromise. A narrow vertical microinstruction holds a pointer into a second memory, the **nanomemory**, whose words are wide horizontal control patterns. Because many microinstructions issue the same control pattern, the nanomemory holds only the *distinct* patterns, and total storage falls sharply. The cost is a second memory access per step, so nanoprogrammed machines are the slowest of the three.

blocks.title: Worked example — sizing a control unit three ways
blocks.text:
A processor needs **42 control signals**. Its control memory holds **1024 microinstructions**, and each microinstruction carries a next-address field plus a 3-bit condition-select field.

**(a) Horizontal.** One bit per signal: 42 bits. Next-address field must address 1024 words, so 10 bits. Plus 3 bits of condition select.

$$\text{width} = 42 + 10 + 3 = 55 \text{ bits}, \qquad \text{control memory} = 1024 \times 55 = 56\,320 \text{ bits} = 6.875\ \text{KB}$$

**(b) Vertical.** Suppose the 42 signals partition into 7 groups of mutually exclusive signals containing 4, 6, 8, 3, 7, 9 and 5 signals respectively (total 42). Each group needs $\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil$ bits:

| Group size $m$ | $m+1$ | bits |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 5 | 3 |
| 6 | 7 | 3 |
| 8 | 9 | 4 |
| 3 | 4 | 2 |
| 7 | 8 | 3 |
| 9 | 10 | 4 |
| 5 | 6 | 3 |

Control field total $= 3+3+4+2+3+4+3 = 22$ bits.

$$\text{width} = 22 + 10 + 3 = 35 \text{ bits}, \qquad 1024 \times 35 = 35\,840 \text{ bits} = 4.375\ \text{KB}$$

A 36% saving in storage, at the cost of seven decoders in the path and a limit of at most seven simultaneous microoperations.

**(c) Nanoprogrammed.** Suppose the 1024 microinstructions issue only **120 distinct** 42-bit control patterns. The nanomemory holds $120 \times 42$ bits, and each microinstruction holds a pointer of $\lceil\log_2 120\rceil = 7$ bits plus the 10-bit address and 3-bit condition field:

$$\text{micromemory} = 1024 \times (7+10+3) = 20\,480 \text{ bits}, \qquad \text{nanomemory} = 120\times 42 = 5040 \text{ bits}$$
$$\text{total} = 25\,520 \text{ bits} \approx 3.1\ \text{KB}$$

Less than half the horizontal design, but every microinstruction now costs two sequential memory reads.

blocks.q: A vertical microinstruction must encode a group of 12 mutually exclusive control signals. The minimum number of bits the field requires is
blocks.exp: The field must encode 12 signals **plus** the possibility that none of them is active, so it needs $\lceil\log_2 13\rceil = 4$ bits. Answering 4 by computing $\lceil\log_2 12\rceil$ happens to give the same number here; the $+1$ matters whenever the group size is an exact power of two — 8 signals need 4 bits, not 3.

blocks.text:
## Tracing a microroutine

The fetch microroutine, in the standard design, occupies three microinstructions at addresses 64–66:

```
ORG 64
FETCH:  PCTAR       U  JMP  NEXT      / AR <- PC
        READ, INCPC U  JMP  NEXT      / DR <- M[AR], PC <- PC+1
        DRTAR       U  MAP            / AR <- DR(0-10), CAR <- mapped opcode
```

The third microinstruction ends with `MAP`, which is how control leaves the fetch routine and enters the routine for whatever opcode was just read.

Each machine instruction's routine then begins with an indirect-addressing test, because the same microcode serves both modes:

```
ADD:    NOP         I  CALL INDRCT    / if I = 1, go and resolve the indirect address
        READ        U  JMP  NEXT      / DR <- M[AR]
        ADD         U  JMP  FETCH     / AC <- AC + DR, then back to fetch

INDRCT: READ        U  JMP  NEXT      / DR <- M[AR]
        DRTAR       U  RET            / AR <- DR(0-10), return to the caller
```

Two observations that are regularly examined. First, the conditional `CALL` costs nothing when $I = 0$ — the condition fails and control simply falls through to $CAR+1$, so direct addressing is free in microinstruction count. Second, `INDRCT` is shared by every memory-reference instruction, which is precisely the economy that microprogramming buys: one copy of a common sequence instead of one per instruction.

## Choosing between the two control styles

| | Hardwired | Microprogrammed |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | faster | slower (control memory access per step) |
| Flexibility | very low — redesign to change | high — rewrite microcode |
| Design cost for complex ISA | very high | moderate |
| Chip area for complex ISA | large, irregular | compact, regular ROM |
| Typical user | RISC | CISC |
| Handling a new instruction | new logic | new microroutine |

Real processors mix the two: common simple instructions are decoded by hardwired logic in one cycle, while rare complex ones trap to microcode.

blocks.q: In a microprogrammed control unit, the mapping logic is used to
opts: increment the control address register after each microinstruction
convert the machine instruction's opcode into the starting address of its microroutine
save the return address during a microsubroutine call
select which status bit a conditional microbranch tests
blocks.exp: Mapping is the bridge from the machine instruction to the microprogram: the opcode bits are transformed (typically padded, as $0\,|\,\text{opcode}\,|\,00$) into a control-memory address where that instruction's microroutine begins. Incrementing is done by the incrementer, return addresses by SBR, and condition selection by the CD field.

tricks.title: A mutually exclusive group of $m$ signals needs $\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil$ bits
tricks.body: The $+1$ encodes 'none active in this group', which every real design needs. It bites exactly when $m$ is a power of two: a group of 8 takes 4 bits, not 3. Sum the fields across groups to get the vertical microinstruction width.

tricks.title: Mapping $0\,|\,\text{opcode}\,|\,00$ means four words per routine
tricks.body: The two appended zeros reserve $2^2 = 4$ consecutive control words for each opcode. Generalise: $k$ appended zeros give $2^k$ words per routine, and the mapped region occupies $2^{\text{opcode bits}+k}$ words of control memory.

tricks.title: CAR width = $\log_2$(control memory words)
tricks.body: And the next-address field must be at least that wide. So 'control memory of 2048 words' immediately gives an 11-bit CAR and an 11-bit AD field, which is usually half of a sizing question's work.

tricks.title: Horizontal = wide and fast, vertical = narrow and slow
tricks.body: Every comparison question reduces to this one axis, because everything else follows: wide means more parallelism, no decoders and more ROM; narrow means fewer simultaneous microoperations, decoder delay and less ROM.

tricks.title: Total control store = words $\times$ width, and width = control field + condition + branch + address
tricks.body: Do not forget the sequencing fields. A question that gives only the number of control signals and the control memory depth still needs the address field, whose width the depth determines.

traps.title: Microprogram is not the same as program
traps.body: A microinstruction executes in one clock period and lives in control memory, which the programmer cannot see or modify. A machine instruction lives in main memory and typically takes several microinstructions. Questions that describe 'a program stored in ROM that the user cannot change' are pointing at the microprogram.

traps.title: Horizontal versus vertical is about encoding, not orientation
traps.body: Nothing is laid out sideways. Horizontal means unencoded, one bit per control signal; vertical means encoded fields plus decoders. A wide microinstruction is a consequence of horizontal encoding, not its definition.

traps.title: Microprogrammed control is slower, not faster
traps.body: It is more flexible and cheaper to design for a complex instruction set, but every microinstruction costs a control-memory read. If a question asks which style gives the faster control unit, the answer is always hardwired.

traps.title: SBR depth limits microsubroutine nesting
traps.body: A single subroutine register allows only one level of microsubroutine call. Nested microroutines require a stack in the sequencer, and a question describing 'a microprogram that calls a routine which calls another' is testing whether you noticed.

topics.title: Central Processing Unit
topics.summary: General register and stack organisations, instruction formats from three-address to zero-address, every addressing mode with a worked effective address, program control, and RISC versus CISC.

blocks.text:
## What the CPU is made of

Three parts: a **register set** that holds intermediate data, an **arithmetic logic unit** that transforms it, and a **control unit** that sequences the whole thing. The interesting design decisions are all about the register set, because they determine the instruction format, the addressing modes and ultimately the size of a program.

## Three organisations

**Single accumulator organisation.** One working register. Every arithmetic instruction names one memory operand and implies the accumulator: `ADD X` means $AC \leftarrow AC + M[X]$. Instructions are short but programs are long, because every intermediate result must be stored and reloaded. This is the basic computer of Unit 2.4.

**General register organisation.** A bank of $n$ registers, any of which can be an operand. Instructions name two or three registers, or a register and a memory location. Intermediate results stay in registers, so programs are much shorter in dynamic instruction count, and the compiler gets a register allocation problem to solve. The register file is typically built as a dual-ported RAM feeding two multiplexers into the ALU, with the result routed back through a bus; the control word that selects "SELA, SELB, OPR, SELD" is itself a micro-level encoding.

**Stack organisation.** Operands are implicit: they are the top elements of a stack. `ADD` pops two, adds, and pushes the result. Instructions carry no address at all, so they are very short, but every operand must first be pushed.

A **stack** in hardware is either a **register stack** — a fixed set of registers with a stack pointer and FULL/EMPTY flags — or a **memory stack**, a region of main memory with a stack-pointer register. For a memory stack growing downward:

$$\text{PUSH}: SP \leftarrow SP - 1,\; M[SP] \leftarrow DR \qquad \text{POP}: DR \leftarrow M[SP],\; SP \leftarrow SP + 1$$

Reverse the order for an upward-growing stack. The **EMPTY** flag is set when SP returns to its base; **FULL** when it reaches the limit. Stack machines evaluate expressions in **reverse Polish (postfix)** notation, which needs no parentheses and no precedence rules: $(A+B) \times (C+D)$ becomes `AB+CD+*`.

blocks.title: Worked example — one expression in four instruction formats
blocks.text:
Evaluate $X = (A + B) \times (C + D)$ on machines with memory operands.

**Three-address.** Each instruction names two sources and a destination.

```
ADD  R1, A, B      / R1 <- M[A] + M[B]
ADD  R2, C, D      / R2 <- M[C] + M[D]
MUL  X,  R1, R2    / M[X] <- R1 * R2
```

**3 instructions.** Shortest program, longest instructions — three address fields per word.

**Two-address.** The destination doubles as a source.

```
MOV  R1, A
ADD  R1, B
MOV  R2, C
ADD  R2, D
MUL  R1, R2
MOV  X,  R1
```

**6 instructions.** This is what x86 and most commercial CISC machines use.

**One-address (accumulator).**

```
LOAD  A
ADD   B
STORE T
LOAD  C
ADD   D
MUL   T
STORE X
```

**7 instructions**, and a temporary memory location `T` is needed because there is only one working register.

**Zero-address (stack).** Convert to postfix first: $AB{+}CD{+}{\times}$.

```
PUSH A
PUSH B
ADD
PUSH C
PUSH D
ADD
MUL
POP  X
```

**8 instructions**, but `ADD`, `MUL` and the arithmetic generally occupy a single byte each, so total program *bytes* can be smaller than the one-address version even though the instruction count is larger. That trade — instruction count versus instruction width — is the whole point of the comparison, and questions ask for the count in a named format rather than the "best" format.

## Addressing modes

An addressing mode says how to compute the **effective address (EA)**, the actual address of the operand. Modes exist for three reasons: to shorten the address field, to support arrays and pointers, and to make code position-independent.

| Mode | Effective address | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Implied** | none — operand is implicit | `CLA`, `CMA`, stack `ADD` |
| **Immediate** | none — the operand *is* the address field | loading constants |
| **Register** | none — operand is in a register | fastest form |
| **Register indirect** | $EA = (R)$ | pointer dereference |
| **Autoincrement** | $EA = (R)$, then $R \leftarrow R+1$ | stepping through an array |
| **Autodecrement** | $R \leftarrow R-1$, then $EA = (R)$ | stack pop, reverse scan |
| **Direct (absolute)** | $EA = \text{address field}$ | global variables |
| **Indirect** | $EA = M[\text{address field}]$ | pointers in memory |
| **Relative (PC-relative)** | $EA = PC + \text{address field}$ | branches, position-independent code |
| **Indexed** | $EA = XR + \text{address field}$ | array element, fixed base |
| **Base register** | $EA = BR + \text{address field}$ | relocation of whole programs |

Indexed and base-register modes compute the same sum; the distinction is one of *intention*. In indexed addressing the address field is the array's fixed base and the index register varies over elements. In base-register addressing the base register holds the segment's relocation constant and the address field is the fixed displacement within it.

Autodecrement decrements **before** forming the address; autoincrement increments **after**. Getting that order backwards moves every access by one element, and it is the difference that questions on pointer arithmetic exploit.

blocks.title: Worked example — every mode on one memory image
blocks.text:
A two-word instruction occupies addresses 200 and 201: the opcode and mode are in word 200 and the address field, value **500**, is in word 201. The next instruction begins at 202, so after the fetch $PC = 202$. Register $R1 = 400$ and the index register $XR = 100$. Memory holds:

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| 200 | opcode + mode |
| 201 | 500 |
| 202 | (next instruction) |
| 399 | 450 |
| 400 | 700 |
| 500 | 800 |
| 600 | 900 |
| 702 | 325 |
| 800 | 300 |

For a `LOAD` instruction, each mode gives:

| Mode | Effective address | Working | Value loaded |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct | 500 | address field used as is | **800** |
| Immediate | 201 | the operand is the address field itself | **500** |
| Indirect | 800 | $M[500] = 800$ | **300** |
| Relative | 702 | $PC + 500 = 202 + 500$ | **325** |
| Indexed | 600 | $XR + 500 = 100 + 500$ | **900** |
| Register | — | operand is $R1$ | **400** |
| Register indirect | 400 | $EA = (R1) = 400$ | **700** |
| Autoincrement | 400 | $EA = (R1) = 400$, then $R1 \to 401$ | **700** |
| Autodecrement | 399 | $R1 \to 399$ first, then $EA = 399$ | **450** |

Three lines deserve a second look.

*Immediate* loads 500, not $M[500]$ — the "effective address" is really the location of the address field itself, which is why some texts say immediate mode has no effective address.

*Relative* uses $PC = 202$, the address of the **next** instruction, because the PC was incremented during fetch. Using 200 or 201 gives 700 or 701 and a completely different answer; this is the single most common error in effective-address questions.

*Autoincrement and autodecrement* differ not only in sign but in **when** the register changes: autoincrement uses the old value (400, giving 700) and autodecrement uses the new value (399, giving 450).

blocks.q: An instruction occupying two words at addresses 300 and 301 uses PC-relative addressing with an address field of $-40$. The effective address is
blocks.exp: The PC is incremented during fetch, so by the time the effective address is computed it points to the next instruction at 302. $EA = PC + \text{offset} = 302 + (-40) = \mathbf{262}$. Using the address of the instruction itself (300) gives 260, which is the planted distractor.

blocks.text:
## Program control

Most instructions leave $PC \leftarrow PC + 1$ alone; program-control instructions change it.

**Status bits** (also called condition codes or flags) are set by the ALU as a side effect of arithmetic:

- $C$ — carry out of the most significant bit
- $S$ (or $N$) — sign, a copy of the result's MSB
- $Z$ — result is zero
- $V$ — signed overflow, computed as $C_n \oplus C_{n-1}$

Conditional branches test these. For **unsigned** comparison after $A - B$: $A > B$ is $C \land \overline{Z}$ for machines where carry means "no borrow", and $A < B$ is $\overline{C}$. For **signed** comparison: $A < B$ is $S \oplus V$, and $A \ge B$ is $\overline{S \oplus V}$. Mixing the signed and unsigned tests is a real bug class and a real exam option.

**Subroutine call** must save the return address. The three historical mechanisms are: a fixed memory location (the basic computer's BSA — no recursion), a register (fast, but must be spilled to nest), and a **stack** (allows arbitrary nesting and recursion, and is what every modern machine does). The stack frame typically holds the return address, saved registers, parameters and local variables.

**Program interrupt** transfers control asynchronously and saves enough state to resume. The three sources:

| Type | Caused by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **External** | outside the CPU | I/O device ready, timer, power fail |
| **Internal (trap/exception)** | the executing instruction itself | divide by zero, invalid opcode, page fault, overflow |
| **Software** | a deliberate instruction | system call, `INT n`, `SVC` |

Internal interrupts are **synchronous** — rerunning the same program with the same data reproduces them at the same point — while external interrupts are asynchronous. That distinction is a standard one-line question.

## RISC versus CISC

**CISC** grew out of the era when memory was expensive and compilers were poor: make instructions powerful so that programs are short and assembly is pleasant to write. **RISC** came from the observation that compilers use only a small subset of those instructions and that a simple, regular machine can be clocked much faster and pipelined much more easily.

| | CISC | RISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction count | large (hundreds) | small (typically under 100) |
| Instruction length | variable | fixed, usually one word |
| Addressing modes | many (12–20) | few (3–5) |
| Memory operands | most instructions can access memory | only **load** and **store** |
| Registers | few (8–16) | many (32+), with register windows in some designs |
| Cycles per instruction | variable, several | close to 1, aided by pipelining |
| Control unit | microprogrammed | hardwired |
| Complexity is in | the hardware | the compiler |

Two RISC features carry their own questions. **Register windows** give each procedure a fresh set of registers that overlaps with its caller's, so parameters pass in the overlap and no memory traffic is needed for the common call depth; only when the windows run out does a spill to memory occur. And the **delayed branch** exposes the pipeline to software: the instruction after a branch executes regardless, so the compiler fills that **delay slot** with useful work instead of a NOP.

The load–store restriction is the deepest difference. Because only loads and stores touch memory, every other instruction has a fixed, short, predictable duration, which is exactly what a clean pipeline needs — the subject of Unit 2.8.

blocks.q: Which sequence correctly evaluates $(A - B) / (C + D \times E)$ on a zero-address stack machine?
opts: `PUSH A, PUSH B, SUB, PUSH C, PUSH D, PUSH E, MUL, ADD, DIV`
`PUSH A, PUSH B, SUB, PUSH C, PUSH D, ADD, PUSH E, MUL, DIV`
`PUSH A, PUSH B, PUSH C, SUB, PUSH D, PUSH E, MUL, ADD, DIV`
`PUSH A, SUB B, PUSH C, MUL D, ADD E, DIV`
blocks.exp: Convert to postfix respecting precedence: $\times$ binds tightest, so $D\,E\,\times$, then $C$ with that sum gives $C\,D\,E\,\times\,+$, and the whole expression is $A\,B\,-\,C\,D\,E\,\times\,+\,\div$. Reading that postfix string with `PUSH` for operands and the bare operator for each symbol gives option 0. Option 1 computes $(C+D)\times E$, and option 3 is not zero-address at all since its instructions carry operands.

tricks.title: Instruction counts: 3-address $\le$ 2-address $<$ 1-address $<$ 0-address
tricks.body: For a binary-operator expression with $k$ operators and no reuse, three-address needs $k$ instructions plus stores, one-address needs roughly $2k+1$, and stack needs one push per operand plus one instruction per operator plus a pop. Count operands and operators rather than writing the program out.

tricks.title: Postfix converts a stack program instantly
tricks.body: Write the expression in reverse Polish; then every operand becomes PUSH and every operator becomes the bare instruction, in the same left-to-right order. Precedence and parentheses vanish, so no bracket-tracking is needed.

tricks.title: Relative addressing always uses the incremented PC
tricks.body: $EA = (\text{address of the following instruction}) + \text{offset}$. If the instruction is two words at 300–301, use 302. This one rule decides most effective-address multiple choices on its own.

tricks.title: Autoincrement uses the old value, autodecrement the new
tricks.body: `(R)+` reads at $R$ then bumps; `-(R)` bumps down then reads. Equivalently, the modification always happens on the side where the minus sign is written. Stack push is `-(SP)` and pop is `(SP)+` on a downward-growing stack.

tricks.title: Indexed and base-register compute the same sum
tricks.body: $EA = \text{register} + \text{displacement}$ for both. If an exam option distinguishes them, the deciding question is which part varies: the register (indexed, walking an array) or the displacement (base, fixed offset into a relocated segment).

traps.title: Immediate mode's operand is the address field
traps.body: Immediate does not fetch from memory at all. If a question tabulates 'effective address' for immediate mode, the answer is the address of the operand field itself (201 in the worked example), and the value loaded is 500 — not $M[500]$.

traps.title: RISC has more registers and fewer addressing modes, not the reverse
traps.body: The whole design moves complexity from hardware to compiler: fewer modes, fixed-length instructions, load–store only, hardwired control, more registers. Options that pair 'RISC' with 'microprogrammed control' or 'variable-length instructions' are always wrong.

traps.title: Signed and unsigned comparisons use different flags
traps.body: After $A-B$, unsigned ordering is read from the carry and zero flags; signed ordering needs $S \oplus V$. A question that compares two bit patterns and asks 'which is greater' is incomplete until the signedness is fixed, and the two readings usually disagree.

traps.title: Stack machines have short instructions, not few instructions
traps.body: Zero-address programs contain **more** instructions than any other format; each one is merely narrower. If a question asks which format minimises program length in bytes, the answer depends on the operand widths and cannot be read off the instruction count alone.

topics.title: Pipeline and Vector Processing
topics.summary: Flynn's taxonomy, arithmetic and instruction pipelines with speedup, efficiency and throughput, the three hazard classes and their remedies, and array and vector processors.

blocks.text:
## Parallelism and Flynn's taxonomy

Parallel processing means doing more than one thing at once in order to raise throughput. The parallelism can be at the bit level (a 32-bit adder rather than a serial one), the instruction level (pipelining, superscalar issue), the data level (one operation applied to many data elements), or the task level (many processors running different programs).

**Flynn's classification** partitions machines by how many instruction streams and how many data streams they support:

| Class | Streams | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SISD** | 1 instruction, 1 data | the classical von Neumann uniprocessor; pipelining still allowed | a single-core scalar CPU |
| **SIMD** | 1 instruction, many data | one control unit broadcasts to many processing elements | array processors, vector units, GPUs |
| **MISD** | many instructions, 1 data | several instruction streams on the same data | essentially none in practice; systolic arrays and redundant fault-tolerant systems are the usual cited cases |
| **MIMD** | many instructions, many data | independent processors on independent data | multicore CPUs, clusters, multiprocessors |

Two points are examined directly. A pipelined uniprocessor is **still SISD** — Flynn counts streams, not overlap. And **MISD is the empty category**; if a question offers it as the answer for a normal parallel machine it is wrong.

## Pipelining: the idea

A pipeline decomposes an operation into $k$ sequential **stages** separated by latches, and lets $k$ different tasks occupy the $k$ stages at once. Each task still takes $k$ stage-times to get through — **latency is not reduced** — but one task *completes* every stage-time once the pipe is full, so **throughput** rises by up to a factor of $k$.

The clock period is set by the slowest stage plus the latch overhead:

$$t_p = \max_i(\tau_i) + t_{latch}$$

which is why balancing stages matters more than shortening the fastest one. A stage twice as slow as its neighbours halves the whole pipeline's rate.

blocks.title: Pipeline performance formulas
blocks.text:
For $n$ tasks through a $k$-stage pipeline with clock period $t_p$, where $t_n$ is the time one task takes on the equivalent non-pipelined unit:

$$T_{pipe} = (k + n - 1)\,t_p \qquad T_{non} = n\,t_n$$

$$\textbf{Speedup } S = \frac{n\,t_n}{(k+n-1)\,t_p} \qquad \textbf{Efficiency } \eta = \frac{S}{k} \qquad \textbf{Throughput } W = \frac{n}{(k+n-1)\,t_p}$$

Throughput is simply tasks completed per unit time, and it approaches $1/t_p$ — one task per clock — as $n$ grows.

**Ideal (perfectly balanced, no latch overhead)**: $t_n = k\,t_p$, so

$$S = \frac{nk}{k+n-1}, \qquad \eta = \frac{n}{k+n-1}, \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty} S = k$$

The $k-1$ in the denominator is the **fill time**: the pipe must be primed before the first result appears, and drained at the end. Its cost is negligible when $n \gg k$ and dominant when $n$ is small.

For an instruction pipeline with stalls, the working formula is

$$CPI = CPI_{ideal} + \text{stall cycles per instruction} = 1 + \sum_{\text{hazards}} (\text{frequency} \times \text{penalty})$$

blocks.title: Worked example — an unbalanced four-stage pipeline
blocks.text:
A processor is divided into four stages with propagation delays 60 ns, 50 ns, 90 ns and 80 ns. Each inter-stage latch costs 10 ns. 1000 instructions are executed.

**Clock period.** $t_p = \max(60,50,90,80) + 10 = 90 + 10 = \mathbf{100\ \text{ns}}$.

**Non-pipelined time per instruction.** Without latches the four stages run back to back: $t_n = 60+50+90+80 = 280$ ns.

**Total times.**
$$T_{non} = 1000 \times 280 = 280\,000\ \text{ns} = 280\ \mu\text{s}$$
$$T_{pipe} = (4 + 1000 - 1)\times 100 = 1003 \times 100 = 100\,300\ \text{ns} = 100.3\ \mu\text{s}$$

**Speedup.**
$$S = \frac{280\,000}{100\,300} = \mathbf{2.79}$$

Not 4, for two separate reasons. The latch adds 10 ns of pure overhead to every stage-time, and the stages are unbalanced: the 50 ns stage idles for 50 ns of every 100 ns clock. The theoretical ceiling here is $t_n / t_p = 280/100 = 2.8$, and we reached 2.79 of it because 1000 is much larger than 4.

**Efficiency.** $\eta = S/k = 2.79/4 = \mathbf{0.698}$. Only 70% of the pipeline's capacity is being used, and the loss is almost entirely imbalance and latch overhead rather than fill time — the pure fill-and-drain utilisation is $n/(k+n-1) = 1000/1003 = 0.997$.

**Throughput.** $1000 / 100\,300\ \text{ns} = 9.97 \times 10^6$ instructions per second $\approx \mathbf{9.97\ \text{MIPS}}$. The non-pipelined machine manages $1/280\,\text{ns} = 3.57$ MIPS.

**What if the stages were balanced?** Repartitioning into four stages of 70 ns each gives $t_p = 80$ ns and $S \to 280/80 = 3.5$, recovering most of the lost speedup without changing the total logic. That is why real designs spend effort on stage balancing.
