blocks.note: Set stage delays, task count and hazard frequency, and watch the space-time diagram, speedup and efficiency change.

blocks.text:
## Arithmetic pipelines

An **arithmetic pipeline** splits one arithmetic operation into stages. The canonical example is floating-point addition, in four stages:

1. **Compare exponents** and compute their difference.
2. **Align mantissas** by shifting the smaller operand's mantissa right by that difference.
3. **Add or subtract** the mantissas.
4. **Normalise** the result and round, adjusting the exponent.

Each stage is roughly equal in delay, which is why the decomposition works. Floating-point multiplication pipelines differently — partial products, carry-save reduction, final add, normalise — and multipliers commonly have deeper pipelines than adders.

## Instruction pipelines

An **instruction pipeline** overlaps the phases of different instructions. The classic five-stage RISC pipeline is

$$\text{IF} \to \text{ID} \to \text{EX} \to \text{MEM} \to \text{WB}$$

(instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute, memory access, write back). A four-stage version merges MEM into EX, and the six-stage instruction pipeline often drawn for this syllabus is FI, DA, FO, EX plus separate decode and write-back stages.

The pipeline runs at full rate only if a new instruction can enter every cycle. Three things prevent that, and they are called **hazards**.

## The three hazard classes

**1. Structural hazard** — two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same cycle. The classic case is a single memory port: an instruction fetch in stage IF collides with a data access in stage MEM. Remedies: duplicate the resource (separate instruction and data caches — the **Harvard** arrangement), pipeline the resource itself, or stall one instruction for a cycle.

**2. Data hazard** — an instruction needs a value that an earlier, still-in-flight instruction has not produced yet. Three dependence types:

| Name | Pattern | Called |
|---|---|---|
| RAW | instruction 2 reads what instruction 1 writes | **true dependence** — a real hazard |
| WAR | instruction 2 writes what instruction 1 reads | anti-dependence |
| WAW | instruction 2 writes what instruction 1 writes | output dependence |

Only **RAW** can occur in a simple in-order pipeline, because writes happen in order in the last stage. WAR and WAW appear only with out-of-order execution or with stages that write early, and both are cured by **register renaming**, since they are naming conflicts rather than genuine data flow.

Remedies for RAW: **operand forwarding (bypassing)**, which routes the ALU result straight from the EX/MEM latch to the next instruction's ALU input, eliminating most stalls; **stalling (interlocking)**, inserting bubbles until the value is ready; and **compiler scheduling**, reordering independent instructions into the gap. Forwarding cannot remove the **load-use** hazard entirely: a value loaded in MEM is available only after MEM, so an instruction immediately after a load that uses its result still stalls one cycle.

**3. Control (branch) hazard** — the next instruction's address is unknown until the branch resolves, so the instructions already fetched may be wrong. If a branch resolves in stage $s$ of a $k$-stage pipeline, a taken branch wastes $s-1$ cycles. Remedies:

- **Stall** until resolution — simple, expensive.
- **Predict not taken** — continue fetching sequentially and squash if wrong.
- **Delayed branch** — define the next instruction to execute regardless, and let the compiler fill the **delay slot**.
- **Branch prediction**, static (always taken, backwards-taken/forwards-not-taken) or dynamic (a branch history table of 1-bit or 2-bit saturating counters). A 2-bit predictor must be wrong twice before changing its prediction, which is why it handles loop back-edges far better than a 1-bit predictor.
- **Branch target buffer**, a cache of recent branch targets so that a predicted-taken branch needs no address computation.

blocks.title: Worked example — CPI with hazards, and the value of prediction
blocks.text:
A 5-stage pipeline has an ideal CPI of 1. In a benchmark, 20% of instructions are branches, 25% are loads, and half of the loads are immediately followed by a dependent instruction. A taken branch costs a 3-cycle penalty; a load-use hazard costs 1 cycle.

**Without prediction (stall on every branch).**

$$CPI = 1 + \underbrace{0.20 \times 3}_{\text{branches}} + \underbrace{0.25 \times 0.5 \times 1}_{\text{load-use}} = 1 + 0.60 + 0.125 = \mathbf{1.725}$$

Speedup over a non-pipelined machine that takes 5 cycles per instruction:

$$S = \frac{5}{1.725} = \mathbf{2.90}$$

**With a predictor that is right 85% of the time.** Only mispredictions cost the 3-cycle penalty:

$$CPI = 1 + 0.20 \times 0.15 \times 3 + 0.125 = 1 + 0.09 + 0.125 = \mathbf{1.215}$$
$$S = \frac{5}{1.215} = \mathbf{4.12}$$

**With prediction and a compiler that fills half the load delay slots.**

$$CPI = 1 + 0.09 + 0.25\times0.25\times1 = 1 + 0.09 + 0.0625 = \mathbf{1.153}, \qquad S = 4.34$$

The lesson the numbers carry: branch penalty dominated the first calculation (0.60 of 0.725 stall cycles), so prediction bought far more than load scheduling did. Attack the largest term first.

blocks.q: A 5-stage pipeline with a 2 ns clock executes 120 instructions with no stalls. The total execution time is
blocks.exp: $T = (k + n - 1)t_p = (5 + 120 - 1)\times 2 = 124 \times 2 = \mathbf{248}$ ns. Forgetting the $k-1$ fill cycles gives 240; multiplying $n \times k \times t_p$ gives 1200, which is the **non-pipelined** time.

blocks.q: Operand forwarding in a classic five-stage pipeline removes the stall for which of the following pairs?
opts: a taken branch followed by the next sequential instruction
two instructions that both write to `R1`
blocks.exp: An ALU result is ready at the end of EX, so it can be forwarded to the next instruction's EX input with no stall — option 1 is fully covered. A load's value is not ready until the end of MEM, so option 0 still costs one bubble even with forwarding. Option 2 is a control hazard and option 3 a WAW naming conflict; neither is what forwarding addresses.

blocks.text:
## Vector and array processors

Scientific code spends most of its time in loops over long arrays, which is a shape the hardware can exploit directly.

A **vector processor** provides instructions whose operands are whole vectors: `V3 ← V1 + V2` adds 64 elements with one instruction fetch and one decode. Three benefits follow. The instruction fetch and loop overhead disappear. The element operations are known to be independent, so they can be fed straight into a deeply pipelined arithmetic unit at one per clock. And the memory accesses are known in advance to be a regular stride, so they can be spread across **interleaved memory banks** — with $m$ banks and a stride coprime to $m$, one element arrives per clock even though each bank is slow.

**Chaining** links vector units so that the output of a multiply pipeline feeds the input of an add pipeline element by element, without waiting for the whole vector. For $\mathbf{c} \leftarrow \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{d}$ this nearly halves the time.

An **array processor** is different. An **attached array processor** is a separate back-end unit that a host CPU hands vector work to. An **SIMD array processor** is a grid of identical **processing elements** (PEs), each with its own local memory, all executing the **same instruction** broadcast by a single control unit, on their own data. Masking registers let a PE sit out an instruction, which is how conditionals are implemented — and why divergent branches waste SIMD throughput. This is the ancestor of the modern GPU.

The distinction asked in exams: a vector processor achieves parallelism **temporally**, by pipelining one functional unit deeply; an array processor achieves it **spatially**, by replicating many functional units. Both are SIMD in Flynn's terms.

blocks.title: Amdahl's law bounds every one of these
blocks.text:
If a fraction $f$ of a program is parallelisable and the rest is strictly serial, then with $p$ processors (or a $p$-fold faster unit)

$$S(p) = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/p}, \qquad \lim_{p\to\infty} S = \frac{1}{1-f}$$

With $f = 0.90$, even infinite parallelism gives only $10\times$. With $f = 0.95$ and $p = 8$: $S = 1/(0.05 + 0.11875) = 5.93$. This is why vector and pipeline speedups quoted for a kernel never translate into the same whole-program speedup, and it reappears in Unit 2.11.

tricks.title: $(k+n-1)$ is the only formula you must recall
tricks.body: Pipelined time is $(k+n-1)t_p$; non-pipelined is $n\,t_n$. Speedup, efficiency and throughput are all ratios built from those two. The $-1$ trips people up: with $n=1$ the pipeline takes exactly $k$ cycles, which is the sanity check.

tricks.title: Clock period = slowest stage + latch, every time
tricks.body: Never average the stage delays. A question listing four unequal stage times is testing exactly this, and the fastest stage's delay is irrelevant except as a hint that the design is unbalanced.

tricks.title: Read the speedup ceiling before computing anything
tricks.body: $S_{max} = t_n / t_p$, achieved as $n \to \infty$. If your computed speedup exceeds it, you have made an arithmetic error; if it is close to it, the fill cost is negligible and you can skip the exact calculation in a hurry.

tricks.title: CPI = 1 + $\sum$ (frequency $\times$ penalty)
tricks.body: Every hazard question reduces to adding stall terms onto an ideal CPI of 1. Then speedup over a non-pipelined machine is $k / CPI$ when the non-pipelined machine takes $k$ cycles per instruction.

tricks.title: Only RAW hazards exist in a simple in-order pipeline
tricks.body: WAR and WAW require out-of-order issue or early writes. If a question describes a plain five-stage in-order pipeline and offers WAR as the answer, it is wrong — and if it describes out-of-order execution, register renaming is the expected remedy.

traps.title: Pipelining reduces throughput time, not latency
traps.body: An individual instruction takes at least as long as before, usually longer because of latch overhead. Speedup is measured on the completion rate for many instructions, so a question about 'the time to execute one instruction' has the opposite answer to one about 'the time to execute 1000'.

traps.title: A pipelined uniprocessor is SISD
traps.body: Flynn classifies by instruction and data streams, not by internal overlap. Superscalar and pipelined machines are still SISD; only replicated data paths under one instruction stream make SIMD.

traps.title: Forwarding does not fix the load-use hazard
traps.body: The loaded value appears only at the end of MEM, one stage too late for the immediately following instruction's EX. One bubble remains, which is why the delay slot after a load exists and why compilers schedule an independent instruction there.

traps.title: MISD has no real examples
traps.body: Every practical parallel machine is SIMD or MIMD. If a question asks which Flynn class has essentially no commercial realisation, the answer is MISD, and selecting it as a description of a vector or multicore machine is wrong.

topics.title: Input-Output Organization
topics.summary: Peripheral interfaces, strobe and handshake asynchronous transfer, programmed, interrupt-driven and DMA transfer modes, priority interrupts and daisy chaining, and serial communication.

blocks.text:
## Why I/O needs its own organisation

Peripherals differ from the CPU in three ways that make a direct connection impossible. They are **slower** by three to six orders of magnitude — a keyboard delivers a few bytes a second, a disk a few hundred megabytes, against a processor executing billions of operations. They use **different data formats and word lengths** — serial bit streams, 8-bit characters, analogue voltages — and often **different electrical levels and timing**. And they are **asynchronous**: nothing synchronises a key press to the processor clock.

The **I/O interface** (device controller) bridges the gap. On the bus side it presents a small set of addressable registers; on the device side it speaks whatever the device speaks. A typical interface has four registers: a **data-out** register, a **data-in** register, a **control** register the CPU writes to issue commands, and a **status** register the CPU reads to learn whether the device is ready or has failed. The interface also contains an **address decoder** and **chip-select** logic so that it responds only to its own addresses, plus buffering and timing conversion.

**Two ways to address I/O registers.**

| | Isolated (I/O-mapped) I/O | Memory-mapped I/O |
|---|---|---|
| Address space | separate I/O space | shares the memory address space |
| Instructions | special `IN` / `OUT` | ordinary `LOAD` / `STORE` |
| Control lines | separate memory-read/write and I/O-read/write | one set |
| Cost | more control logic, full memory space available | loses some memory addresses to devices |
| Flexibility | only the special instructions can touch devices | the full instruction set, including bit operations, works on device registers |

Memory-mapped I/O is what nearly every modern machine uses, precisely because the full instruction set becomes available on device registers.

## Asynchronous data transfer

When source and destination have independent clocks, they must agree on when data is valid. There are two standard schemes.

**Strobe control** uses a single control line. In a **source-initiated** transfer the source places data on the bus, waits for it to settle, then pulses the strobe; the destination latches on the strobe edge and the source removes the data after a delay. In a **destination-initiated** transfer the destination pulses the strobe first as a request, and the source responds with data.

The weakness of a strobe is fatal for slow or unreliable devices: **there is no acknowledgement**. The source cannot tell whether the destination was ready, and the destination cannot tell whether the data is fresh.

**Handshaking** fixes this by adding a second control line so that each side confirms. In the **source-initiated** version:

1. The source places data on the bus and asserts **data valid**.
2. The destination sees data valid, reads the data, and asserts **data accepted**.
3. The source sees data accepted and de-asserts data valid, removing the data.
4. The destination sees data valid go away and de-asserts data accepted.

The cycle is now complete and a fresh one can start. In the **destination-initiated** version the destination asserts **ready for data** first and the source replies with **data valid**. Either way, **two control lines and a four-phase sequence** are the signature of handshaking, and the benefit is that a timeout at any step reveals an error, which a strobe cannot do.

## The three modes of transfer

**Programmed I/O.** The CPU executes an instruction to test the device's status flag, loops until it is ready, and then executes an instruction to move one word between the interface and a register, and another to move it to memory. Simple, requires no extra hardware, and **wastes the entire CPU** on waiting. Suitable only for very slow devices or very small transfers.

**Interrupt-driven I/O.** The device raises an interrupt when it is ready. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the PC (and usually the status register), and jumps to a service routine that performs the transfer. The polling loop is gone, so the CPU does useful work between transfers, but **every word still costs an interrupt** — plus context save and restore, which is far more expensive than the transfer itself.

**Direct memory access (DMA).** A **DMA controller** is given a starting memory address, a word count and a direction, and then moves the whole block between the device and memory **without the CPU**, raising a single interrupt when the block is done. To do this it must become bus master, which it requests with a **bus request (BR)** line and is granted with **bus grant (BG)**; the CPU then floats its address, data and control lines onto high impedance.

Two DMA transfer styles:

- **Cycle stealing (single-word)** — the controller takes one memory cycle at a time, returning the bus between words. The CPU is slowed but never stopped. This is the usual mode.
- **Burst (block) transfer** — the controller holds the bus for the whole block. Fastest for the device, but the CPU stalls for the duration, so it suits high-rate devices like disks reading a full sector.

A DMA controller's registers are an **address register** (incremented after each word), a **word count register** (decremented, and the transfer ends when it reaches zero), and a **control register** holding direction and mode.

Beyond DMA, an **I/O processor (IOP)** or **channel** is a small processor with its own instruction set that executes a *channel program* in main memory, handling several devices and complex sequences with no CPU involvement at all. A **selector channel** serves one high-speed device at a time; a **multiplexer channel** interleaves many slow devices.

blocks.title: Worked example — comparing the three modes on a disk
blocks.text:
A disk transfers data at $2 \times 10^6$ bytes per second. The memory bus moves 4 bytes per cycle and a memory cycle is 100 ns. An interrupt costs 2 $\mu$s of CPU time including save and restore; a DMA block interrupt costs 10 $\mu$s. Blocks are 4096 bytes.

**Interrupt-driven, one byte per interrupt.**

$$\text{interrupts/s} = 2\times10^6, \qquad \text{CPU time/s} = 2\times10^6 \times 2\,\mu\text{s} = 4\ \text{s}$$

Four seconds of CPU work per second of real time — the device simply cannot be serviced this way. Even at one interrupt per 4-byte word it would need 1 s per second, i.e. 100% of the CPU.

**DMA with cycle stealing.**

Words transferred per second $= 2\times10^6 / 4 = 500\,000$. Each steals one 100 ns memory cycle:

$$\text{memory time stolen} = 500\,000 \times 100\ \text{ns} = 0.05\ \text{s per second} = \mathbf{5\%}$$

of memory bandwidth. The CPU is not stopped; it merely waits when it happens to want memory in a stolen cycle.

**CPU cost of DMA interrupts.**

$$\text{blocks/s} = \frac{2\times10^6}{4096} = 488.3, \qquad \text{CPU time} = 488.3 \times 10\,\mu\text{s} = 4.88\ \text{ms per second} = \mathbf{0.49\%}$$

So DMA reduces the processor's share of this transfer from an impossible 400% to under half a percent, at the price of 5% of memory bandwidth and one extra controller.

**How large must a block be for DMA to beat interrupts?** Break-even is when DMA's per-block cost equals the interrupt scheme's per-byte cost over the same block: $10\,\mu\text{s} = B \times 2\,\mu\text{s}$, so $B = 5$ bytes. Any block above five bytes favours DMA — which is why DMA is used for essentially every block device.

blocks.q: During a DMA transfer in cycle-stealing mode, the CPU
opts: is halted until the entire block has been transferred
continues executing but occasionally waits for a memory cycle taken by the DMA controller
polls the DMA controller's status register after every word
transfers each word itself under the DMA controller's direction
blocks.exp: Cycle stealing takes the bus for one memory cycle at a time and releases it, so the CPU keeps running and is delayed only when it wants memory in a cycle the controller has taken. Option 0 describes **burst** mode. The whole point of DMA is that the CPU neither polls nor moves the data.

blocks.text:
## Priority interrupts

With several devices able to interrupt, the system must decide which to serve first and must tell the CPU where the service routine is. Three mechanisms appear in questions.

**Software polling.** One common interrupt line; the service routine tests each device's status in a fixed order. Priority is the polling order, so it is trivially changed in software, but the time to identify the device grows with the number of devices, and the last device polled has the worst latency.

**Daisy chaining (serial hardware priority).** All devices share one interrupt request line. A **priority-in (PI)** / **priority-out (PO)** chain runs from the CPU through the devices in priority order. The rule at each device is:

- If $PI = 0$, the device is blocked: it sets $PO = 0$ and does not respond.
- If $PI = 1$ and the device is **not** requesting, it passes the grant along: $PO = 1$.
- If $PI = 1$ and the device **is** requesting, it takes the grant, sets $PO = 0$ (blocking everything downstream), and places its **vector address (VAD)** on the data bus.

So $PO = PI \cdot \overline{RF}$ where $RF$ is the device's request flag. Priority is fixed by physical position in the chain: **nearest the CPU wins**. The scheme is cheap — one extra line per device — but the grant must ripple through every device, so the delay grows linearly with chain length, and a failed device breaks the chain for everything behind it.

**Parallel priority interrupt.** Each device has a bit in an **interrupt register** and a corresponding bit in a **mask register**; the ANDed result feeds a **priority encoder** whose output is the index of the highest-priority active request. That index forms the vector address, and an **interrupt status flip-flop (IST)** signals the CPU. Priority is now fixed by the encoder but individual devices can be disabled through the mask, and — crucially — the mask can be changed inside a service routine to allow **higher-priority interrupts to nest** while blocking equal and lower ones. Resolution is in constant time regardless of the number of devices.

**Vectored interrupts** in all these schemes mean that the interrupting device supplies an address (or an index into an interrupt vector table) so the CPU branches straight to the right routine, rather than polling to find out who called.

blocks.q: In a daisy-chain priority system, device 3 has $PI = 1$ and is requesting an interrupt. What are its $PO$ output and the consequence for device 4, which is further from the CPU?
blocks.exp: A device that receives $PI = 1$ and is itself requesting seizes the grant and drives $PO = 0$, since $PO = PI \cdot \overline{RF}$ and $RF = 1$. Every device downstream therefore sees $PI = 0$ and is blocked. This is exactly why position in the chain determines priority, with the device nearest the CPU highest.

blocks.text:
## Serial communication

Parallel transfer needs one wire per bit and is limited to short distances by skew and cost, so anything going more than a metre or two goes **serial**.

**Asynchronous serial transfer** sends one character at a time with no shared clock. The line idles at logic 1. A character frame is:

$$\underbrace{0}_{\text{start}} \;\; \underbrace{d_0 d_1 \dots d_{n-1}}_{5\text{–}8\text{ data bits, LSB first}} \;\; \underbrace{p}_{\text{optional parity}} \;\; \underbrace{1\ (1,\ 1.5\ \text{or}\ 2)}_{\text{stop}}$$

The receiver detects the falling edge of the start bit, waits half a bit time to sample at the centre, and then samples every bit time. Because resynchronisation happens at every character, only modest clock accuracy is needed — but the framing bits are pure overhead: an 8-data-bit character with one start and one stop bit costs **10 bits per 8 bits of data**, a 20% loss.

**Baud rate** is signalling elements per second; **bit rate** is bits per second. They are equal only when one signalling element carries one bit. With an 8-bit character, no parity and one stop bit, a 9600-baud line carries $9600/10 = 960$ characters per second.

**Synchronous serial transfer** sends a continuous stream with the clock recovered from the data, preceded by SYN characters (character-oriented protocols such as BSC) or by a flag pattern `01111110` with **bit stuffing** to prevent the flag appearing in the data (bit-oriented protocols such as HDLC/SDLC). Removing the per-character framing makes synchronous transmission much more efficient at high rates.

**Direction modes:** **simplex** (one direction only), **half-duplex** (both directions but not at once, requiring line turnaround), **full-duplex** (both directions simultaneously, needing two channels or frequency division).

The interface chip that does all this is a **UART** (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter), which contains a transmitter shift register with framing logic, a receiver shift register with a clock divided typically 16 times the baud rate for centre sampling, and status bits for **parity error**, **framing error** (a stop bit found to be 0) and **overrun error** (a character arrived before the previous one was read).

blocks.title: Serial throughput arithmetic
blocks.text:
For asynchronous serial with $d$ data bits, $s$ stop bits and optional parity:

$$\text{bits per character} = 1 + d + p + s$$
$$\text{characters per second} = \frac{\text{bit rate}}{\text{bits per character}}, \qquad \text{efficiency} = \frac{d}{1+d+p+s}$$

At 1200 bps with 7 data bits, even parity and 2 stop bits: $1+7+1+2 = 11$ bits per character, so $1200/11 = 109$ characters per second and efficiency $7/11 = 63.6\%$. Switching to 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit gives $1200/10 = 120$ characters per second at $80\%$ efficiency on the same line.

tricks.title: Handshaking has two control lines; strobe has one
tricks.body: That single fact decides most asynchronous-transfer questions. Two lines means each side acknowledges, so errors and timeouts are detectable; one line means fire-and-forget. 'Source-initiated' versus 'destination-initiated' only says who moves first.

tricks.title: DMA cost splits into bandwidth and interrupts
tricks.body: Compute stolen memory cycles (words per second $\times$ cycle time) for the **bandwidth** cost, and blocks per second $\times$ interrupt cost for the **CPU** cost. Questions usually want one or the other, and mixing them produces an answer thousands of times too large or too small.

tricks.title: $PO = PI \cdot \overline{RF}$ solves any daisy-chain question
tricks.body: Walk the chain from the CPU: a non-requesting device passes the grant on, a requesting device with $PI=1$ takes it and kills everything downstream, and a device with $PI=0$ is dead. Nothing else is needed.

tricks.title: Asynchronous serial: divide the bit rate by the frame size
tricks.body: Frame size is $1 + \text{data} + \text{parity} + \text{stop}$. The classic 8-N-1 frame is 10 bits, so characters per second is simply bit rate over 10 — and efficiency is exactly 80%.

tricks.title: Memory-mapped I/O uses ordinary load and store
tricks.body: If a question describes accessing a device with `MOV` or with bit-manipulation instructions, or mentions that part of the address space is reserved for devices, it is memory-mapped. Special `IN`/`OUT` instructions and a separate I/O address space mean isolated I/O.

traps.title: Interrupt-driven I/O still moves every word through the CPU
traps.body: Removing the polling loop is not the same as removing the transfer. Each word costs an interrupt, a context save and a restore, so interrupt-driven I/O is often **slower per byte** than programmed I/O for a fast device — its benefit is that the CPU does other work in between.

traps.title: Cycle stealing does not halt the CPU
traps.body: Only burst mode holds the bus for the whole block. In cycle-stealing mode the CPU keeps executing and merely contends for memory, which is why a 5% bandwidth cost does not mean a 5% slower program — it is usually less, since not every CPU cycle wants memory.

traps.title: Daisy-chain priority is fixed by wiring, not by software
traps.body: You cannot re-prioritise a daisy chain without moving devices. Software-changeable priority requires the mask-register-plus-priority-encoder scheme, or plain software polling. Questions offering 'daisy chaining allows dynamic priority' are wrong.

traps.title: Baud and bits per second are not synonyms
traps.body: They coincide only for binary signalling with one bit per symbol. With multilevel modulation a 2400-baud line can carry 9600 bps. And even when they coincide, the **character** rate is lower still, because of start, stop and parity bits.

topics.title: Memory Hierarchy
topics.summary: The speed-cost-capacity hierarchy, associative memory, cache mapping and address splitting, hit ratios and effective access time, and virtual memory with page tables and TLBs.

blocks.text:
## The hierarchy and why it works

No single memory technology is simultaneously fast, large and cheap. Registers built from flip-flops take a fraction of a nanosecond but there are only a few dozen; disks hold terabytes but take milliseconds. The resolution is a **hierarchy**, with small fast expensive memory near the processor and large slow cheap memory far from it, arranged so that most references are satisfied near the top.

| Level | Typical access | Typical size | Managed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | < 1 ns | hundreds of bytes | compiler |
| L1 cache | 1–2 ns | 32–64 KB | hardware |
| L2 / L3 cache | 5–30 ns | 256 KB – 32 MB | hardware |
| Main memory | 50–100 ns | 8–64 GB | operating system |
| Solid-state disk | 50–100 $\mu$s | 0.5–4 TB | operating system |
| Magnetic disk / tape | 5–10 ms / seconds | terabytes | operating system |

The hierarchy works only because programs exhibit **locality of reference**:

- **Temporal locality** — a location referenced now is likely to be referenced again soon (loop bodies, counters, the top of the stack).
- **Spatial locality** — locations near one just referenced are likely to be referenced soon (sequential code, array traversal, adjacent fields of a record).

Temporal locality justifies *keeping* a word once fetched; spatial locality justifies fetching a whole **block** around it. Without locality, a cache would be useless, and the programs that defeat caches — random pointer chasing, column-major traversal of a row-major array — are exactly the ones with poor locality.

**Main memory** is semiconductor RAM: **DRAM** (one transistor and one capacitor per bit, dense, cheap, needs refreshing every few milliseconds, slower) for the bulk, and **SRAM** (six transistors per bit, no refresh, fast, expensive, less dense) for caches. **ROM**, **PROM**, **EPROM**, **EEPROM** and flash hold the bootstrap loader and firmware, which must survive power-off. **Auxiliary memory** — disks, SSDs, tape — is non-volatile, block-addressed rather than byte-addressed, and outside the processor's address space.

Disk access time decomposes as $\text{seek time} + \text{rotational latency} + \text{transfer time}$, with average rotational latency equal to half a revolution.

## Associative (content-addressable) memory

An ordinary memory is addressed by location. An **associative memory**, or **content-addressable memory (CAM)**, is addressed by **content**: you present a data pattern and it reports which words match, in a single access, because every word has its own comparison logic.

The organisation is: an **argument register $A$** holding the pattern to search for, a **key register $K$** masking which bits of the argument take part, a **match register $M$** with one bit per word, and the cell array itself. Word $i$ sets $M_i$ if it agrees with $A$ in every bit position where $K$ has a 1:

$$M_i = \prod_j \left( \overline{K_j} + \overline{(A_j \oplus F_{ij})} \right)$$

Searching is $O(1)$ regardless of the number of words, against $O(\log n)$ for a binary search of sorted conventional memory. The cost is the comparison logic in every cell, which makes CAM several times larger and more power-hungry per bit than SRAM — which is why it is used only where the search must be instantaneous and the table is small: **TLBs**, fully associative cache tag stores, and network routing tables.

## Cache memory and the three mapping functions

A cache holds copies of recently used main-memory blocks. When the CPU issues an address, the cache checks whether the containing block is present: a **hit** is served at cache speed, a **miss** fetches the whole block from memory.

Main memory is divided into blocks of $B$ bytes; the cache is divided into the same-sized **lines**. Every address splits into fields whose widths follow mechanically from the geometry.

$$\text{offset bits} = \log_2 B \qquad \text{number of lines} = \frac{\text{cache size}}{B} \qquad \text{sets} = \frac{\text{lines}}{\text{associativity}}$$

$$\text{index bits} = \log_2(\text{sets}) \qquad \text{tag bits} = \text{address bits} - \text{index bits} - \text{offset bits}$$

**Direct mapping** — one possible line per block, chosen by $\text{block number} \bmod \text{lines}$. Simplest and fastest to check (one tag comparison), but two hot blocks that map to the same line evict each other repeatedly: a **conflict miss**. Here associativity is 1, so sets = lines.

**Fully associative mapping** — a block may go in any line. No conflict misses at all, but every tag must be compared in parallel, which needs a CAM and limits the practical size. Here there is **one set**, so there are **no index bits** and the tag is the whole block number.

**Set-associative mapping** — the compromise. Lines are grouped into sets of $k$; a block maps to exactly one set and may occupy any of the $k$ lines in it. $k$ comparators are needed. Nearly all real caches are 2-, 4-, 8- or 16-way.

**Replacement** matters only when there is a choice, so direct-mapped caches need no replacement policy at all. For the others: **LRU** (best hit rate, expensive beyond 4-way), **FIFO**, **random** (surprisingly competitive), and **LFU**.

**Write policy**: **write-through** updates cache and memory together — simple, keeps memory consistent, but generates traffic on every write; a **write buffer** hides most of the latency. **Write-back** updates only the cache and marks the line **dirty**, writing it to memory on eviction — far less traffic, but memory is stale, which matters for DMA and multiprocessors (Unit 2.11). On a write miss, **write-allocate** fetches the block first (pairs naturally with write-back) while **no-write-allocate** writes straight to memory (pairs with write-through).

**The three Cs of cache misses**: **compulsory** (first reference to a block, unavoidable except by prefetching), **capacity** (the working set exceeds the cache), **conflict** (too many blocks map to one set; zero in a fully associative cache).

blocks.title: Worked example — splitting an address three ways
blocks.text:
A byte-addressable machine has **32-bit addresses**, a **256 KB** cache with **64-byte** blocks.

**Common quantities.** $\text{offset} = \log_2 64 = \mathbf{6}$ bits. Number of lines $= 262144/64 = \mathbf{4096}$.

**(a) Direct mapped.** Sets = lines = 4096, so index $= \log_2 4096 = 12$ bits, and tag $= 32 - 12 - 6 = \mathbf{14}$ bits.

**(b) 8-way set associative.** Sets $= 4096/8 = 512$, so index $= 9$ bits, and tag $= 32 - 9 - 6 = \mathbf{17}$ bits.

**(c) Fully associative.** One set, so no index bits, and tag $= 32 - 0 - 6 = \mathbf{26}$ bits.

Notice the pattern: **doubling the associativity removes one index bit and adds one tag bit**, leaving the offset alone.

**Where does address `0x1A2B3C4D` land in the 8-way cache?** In binary,

$$\texttt{0001 1010 0010 1011 0011 1100 0100 1101}$$

- Offset = low 6 bits = $001101_2 = 13$.
- Index = next 9 bits = $0\,1111\,0001_2 = 241$, so **set 241**.
- Tag = top 17 bits = $\texttt{0x3456} = 13398$.

In the **direct-mapped** cache the same address gives offset 13, index = next 12 bits = $\texttt{0xCF1} = 3313$ (**line 3313**), tag = top 14 bits = $\texttt{0x68A} = 1674$.

**Tag store overhead for the 8-way cache.** Each line needs its 17 tag bits plus a valid bit plus a dirty bit (write-back):

$$4096 \times (17+1+1) = 4096 \times 19 = 77\,824 \text{ bits} = 9728 \text{ bytes} = 9.5\ \text{KB}$$

which is 3.7% on top of the 256 KB of data — the standard answer to "why not make blocks smaller".

**Why fully associative costs more.** Its 26-bit tags over 4096 lines need $4096\times28 = 114\,688$ bits, 47% more tag storage, plus 4096 comparators instead of 8.

blocks.title: Try it — cache mapping and hit ratio
blocks.note: Set the cache size, block size and associativity, feed an address trace, and watch the tag/index/offset split and the hit ratio.

blocks.title: Hit ratio and effective access time
blocks.text:
$$h = \frac{\text{hits}}{\text{hits}+\text{misses}}, \qquad \text{miss ratio} = 1 - h$$

**Simultaneous (parallel / look-aside) access** — cache and memory are started together, so a miss costs only the memory time:

$$T_{eff} = h\,t_c + (1-h)\,t_m$$

**Hierarchical (sequential / look-through) access** — memory is consulted only after the cache reports a miss:

$$T_{eff} = h\,t_c + (1-h)(t_c + t_m) = t_c + (1-h)\,t_m$$

For **two levels of cache** with sequential access:

$$T_{eff} = t_{L1} + (1-h_1)\big[t_{L2} + (1-h_2)\,t_m\big]$$

where $h_2$ is the **local** hit ratio of L2 (hits in L2 divided by references that reach L2). If a question gives a *global* L2 hit ratio instead, use it directly against the total reference count rather than nesting it.

The two conventions differ by exactly $(1-h)\,t_c$, since $\big[t_c + (1-h)t_m\big] - \big[h\,t_c + (1-h)t_m\big] = (1-h)t_c$. The exam normally intends the **hierarchical** formula unless it states that cache and memory are started together; when a question gives only "cache 10 ns, memory 100 ns", solve with the hierarchical form and check whether the simultaneous value also appears among the options.

blocks.title: Worked example — effective access time and the cost of a miss
blocks.text:
A cache has access time 10 ns, main memory 100 ns, and a hit ratio of 0.95.

**Hierarchical:** $T_{eff} = 10 + 0.05\times100 = \mathbf{15\ \text{ns}}$.

**Simultaneous:** $T_{eff} = 0.95\times10 + 0.05\times100 = 9.5 + 5 = \mathbf{14.5\ \text{ns}}$.

Either way the cache has turned a 100 ns memory into an effective 15 ns memory — a speedup of $100/15 = 6.7$.

**How sensitive is this to the hit ratio?** Using the hierarchical formula:

| $h$ | $T_{eff}$ |
|---|---|
| 0.99 | $10 + 0.01\times100 = 11$ ns |
| 0.95 | 15 ns |
| 0.90 | 20 ns |
| 0.80 | 30 ns |

Dropping from 99% to 90% hits **doubles** the effective access time, because misses cost ten times a hit. This non-linearity is why cache design obsesses over the last percent of hit rate, and why questions often ask for the hit ratio required to meet a target.

**Solving backwards.** What hit ratio gives $T_{eff} = 12$ ns?

$$12 = 10 + (1-h)\times100 \;\Rightarrow\; 1-h = 0.02 \;\Rightarrow\; h = \mathbf{0.98}$$

**Two-level cache.** L1: 2 ns, 90% hit. L2: 10 ns, 80% local hit. Memory: 100 ns.

$$T_{eff} = 2 + 0.10\big[10 + 0.20\times100\big] = 2 + 0.10\times30 = \mathbf{5\ \text{ns}}$$

Only 10% of references reach L2 and only 2% reach memory, so the 100 ns memory contributes just $0.02\times100 = 2$ ns of the total.

blocks.q: A 16 KB 4-way set-associative cache has 32-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. The number of tag bits is
blocks.exp: Offset $= \log_2 32 = 5$ bits. Lines $= 16384/32 = 512$; sets $= 512/4 = 128$, so index $= \log_2 128 = 7$ bits. Tag $= 32 - 7 - 5 = \mathbf{18}$. The common error is to use the line count rather than the set count for the index, giving 9 index bits and a tag of 16.

blocks.text:
## Virtual memory

Virtual memory gives each process a private **virtual address space** larger than physical memory, with the operating system and the memory management unit translating virtual addresses to physical ones and moving pages between memory and disk on demand. Three benefits follow: programs larger than RAM can run, processes are isolated from each other, and physical memory can be allocated in non-contiguous frames, removing external fragmentation.

**Paging.** The virtual address space is divided into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into equal-sized **frames**. A virtual address splits as

$$\underbrace{\text{page number}}_{\text{high bits}} \;\Vert\; \underbrace{\text{offset}}_{\log_2(\text{page size}) \text{ bits}}$$

and the **page table** maps page number to frame number, leaving the offset unchanged. Each **page table entry (PTE)** holds the frame number plus valid, dirty (modified), referenced and protection bits.

The page table itself is large: a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages has $2^{32}/2^{12} = 2^{20}$ pages, so a 4-byte PTE gives a **4 MB page table per process**, too big to keep resident. The remedies are **multi-level page tables** (split the 20-bit page number into 10 + 10, so only the outer table and the in-use inner tables need be resident) and **inverted page tables** (one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page, so the size depends on physical memory, at the cost of needing a hash to search).

**The TLB.** Every virtual reference would need one memory access for the page table plus one for the data, doubling the cost. The **translation lookaside buffer** is a small fully associative (or highly associative) cache of recent page-table entries, holding perhaps 64 to 1024 translations. A TLB hit makes translation nearly free.

$$T_{eff} = h_{TLB}(t_{TLB} + t_m) + (1-h_{TLB})(t_{TLB} + 2t_m)$$

for a single-level page table, because a TLB miss costs one extra memory access to read the PTE. With a $k$-level page table the miss path costs $k$ extra accesses.

On a **context switch** the TLB entries of the old process are invalid, so the TLB is flushed — unless entries carry an **address space identifier (ASID)**, which lets several processes' translations coexist.

**Segmentation** divides the address space by *logical* unit — code, data, stack, a table — into variable-length **segments**, each with a base and a limit. It matches the programmer's view and makes protection and sharing natural at the level of a whole module, but variable sizes reintroduce **external fragmentation**. **Segmented paging** combines both: a segment is divided into pages, so protection and sharing are per-segment while allocation is per-page.

**Memory management hardware** adds: base and limit (bounds) registers for relocation and protection; per-page or per-segment access rights (read / write / execute), checked on every reference; and a **page fault** trap when the valid bit is 0, which suspends the instruction, lets the OS fetch the page, and restarts the instruction.

blocks.title: Worked example — address translation and TLB timing
blocks.text:
A system has **32-bit virtual addresses**, **4 KB pages**, and **1 GB of physical memory**. PTEs are 4 bytes.

**Field widths.** Offset $= \log_2 4096 = \mathbf{12}$ bits, so the virtual page number is $32-12 = \mathbf{20}$ bits. Physical memory of $2^{30}$ bytes holds $2^{30}/2^{12} = 2^{18}$ frames, so the frame number is **18 bits** and the physical address is $18+12 = 30$ bits.

**Single-level page table size.** $2^{20}$ entries $\times$ 4 bytes $= \mathbf{4\ \text{MB}}$ per process.

**Two-level page table.** Split the 20-bit page number as $10 + 10$. The outer table has $2^{10}$ entries $\times$ 4 bytes $= 4$ KB — conveniently exactly one page — and each inner table likewise 4 KB. A process touching only 16 MB of address space needs the 4 KB outer table plus $16\,\text{MB}/4\,\text{MB} = 4$ inner tables, so $5 \times 4\,\text{KB} = \mathbf{20\ \text{KB}}$ instead of 4 MB.

**Translate `0x00403ABC`.** In binary the low 12 bits are the offset: $\texttt{0xABC} = 2748$. The page number is the top 20 bits, $\texttt{0x00403} = 1027$. Under the two-level split, the outer index is the top 10 bits ($\texttt{0x00403ABC} \gg 22 = 1$) and the inner index the next 10 bits ($(\texttt{0x00403ABC} \gg 12)\,\&\,1023 = 3$). If page 1027 maps to frame $\texttt{0x2F1}$, the physical address is $\texttt{0x2F1}$ shifted left 12 with the offset appended: $\texttt{0x002F1ABC}$.

**Effective access time.** TLB access 10 ns, memory 100 ns, TLB hit ratio 90%, single-level page table:

$$T_{eff} = 0.9(10+100) + 0.1(10+100+100) = 0.9\times110 + 0.1\times210 = 99 + 21 = \mathbf{120\ \text{ns}}$$

With a **two-level** table the miss path needs two page-table accesses:

$$T_{eff} = 0.9\times110 + 0.1(10 + 200 + 100) = 99 + 31 = \mathbf{130\ \text{ns}}$$

so the 4 MB of saved table costs 10 ns per average reference — and raising the TLB hit ratio to 98% brings it back down to $0.98\times110 + 0.02\times310 = 107.8 + 6.2 = 114$ ns, better than the single-level version at 90%.

blocks.q: Cache access time is 20 ns and main memory access time is 200 ns, with accesses made hierarchically (memory consulted only after a cache miss). What hit ratio gives an effective access time of 40 ns?
blocks.exp: $T_{eff} = t_c + (1-h)t_m$, so $40 = 20 + (1-h)\times200$, giving $(1-h) = 20/200 = 0.1$ and $h = \mathbf{0.90}$. Under the simultaneous convention the equation would be $40 = 20h + 200(1-h)$, giving $h = 0.889$ — not among the options, which confirms the hierarchical reading is intended.

tricks.title: Split the address from the right
tricks.body: Offset first ($\log_2$ block size), then index ($\log_2$ **sets**, not lines), and the tag is whatever remains. Sets $=$ lines $/$ associativity, so direct-mapped means sets $=$ lines and fully associative means sets $= 1$ with **no** index field.

tricks.title: Doubling associativity moves one bit from index to tag
tricks.body: Block size and cache size fixed, going 1-way $\to$ 2-way $\to$ 4-way shifts one index bit into the tag each time. Useful for checking an answer instantly, and for answering 'how do the fields change if…' questions without recomputing.

tricks.title: $T_{eff} = t_c + (1-h)t_m$ for hierarchical access
tricks.body: This collapsed form avoids arithmetic slips and makes backwards questions trivial: given a target $T_{eff}$, the required miss ratio is $(T_{eff}-t_c)/t_m$. Use $h\,t_c + (1-h)t_m$ only when the question says cache and memory are started simultaneously.

tricks.title: Page-table size = (virtual pages) $\times$ (entry size)
tricks.body: Virtual pages $= 2^{\text{VA bits} - \log_2(\text{page size})}$. Physical memory size never enters this calculation — it only fixes the **width of the frame number** inside each entry, which is the other half of the standard question.

tricks.title: TLB miss adds one memory access per page-table level
tricks.body: $T_{eff} = h(t_{TLB}+t_m) + (1-h)(t_{TLB} + (k{+}1)t_m)$ for a $k$-level table. Write the two paths out rather than memorising a formula; the hit path is always 'look up, then fetch the data'.

traps.title: Index bits come from the number of sets, not lines
traps.body: In a $k$-way cache there are lines$/k$ sets. Using the line count inflates the index and shrinks the tag by exactly $\log_2 k$ bits, and the wrong answer is always one of the options.

traps.title: Fully associative caches have no index field
traps.body: Every block can go anywhere, so there is nothing to index. The tag is the whole block number, address bits minus offset bits. Answering 'tag = address − index − offset' with a non-zero index here is the planted mistake.

traps.title: Direct-mapped caches need no replacement policy
traps.body: There is exactly one candidate line, so LRU, FIFO and random are all meaningless. A question offering 'LRU' as the policy of a direct-mapped cache is testing whether you noticed that the choice does not exist.

traps.title: Cache blocks and virtual pages are different partitions
traps.body: A block is typically 32–128 bytes and is the unit of transfer between memory and cache; a page is typically 4 KB and is the unit of transfer between disk and memory. Questions that give both numbers expect you to keep the two address splits separate.

traps.title: Page-table size does not depend on physical memory
traps.body: A process with a 32-bit virtual address space and 4 KB pages has $2^{20}$ page-table entries whether the machine has 256 MB or 64 GB installed. The physical size only sets how many bits of each entry hold the frame number.

topics.title: Multiprocessors
topics.summary: Tightly and loosely coupled systems, interconnection networks and their switch counts, bus arbitration, synchronisation primitives, cache coherence protocols and multicore design.

blocks.text:
## What a multiprocessor is

A **multiprocessor** is a single computer system containing two or more processors that share access to a common memory and are controlled by one operating system. In Flynn's terms it is **MIMD**: each processor fetches its own instruction stream and works on its own data.

The reasons for building one are throughput (run many jobs at once), speedup of a single parallel job, reliability through redundancy (a failed processor degrades performance rather than stopping the system), and cost — many modest processors are cheaper per unit of performance than one very fast one, because single-thread performance runs into power and clock-frequency walls.

**Tightly coupled versus loosely coupled** is the first classification.

| | Tightly coupled (shared memory) | Loosely coupled (distributed memory) |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | one shared physical address space | private memory per node |
| Communication | shared variables | message passing |
| Latency | tens of nanoseconds | microseconds to milliseconds |
| Scalability | limited by memory contention (tens of processors) | very high (thousands of nodes) |
| Usual name | **multiprocessor** | **multicomputer**, cluster |

Within shared-memory machines, the access-time structure matters:

- **UMA (uniform memory access)** — every processor reaches every memory word in the same time. The classic symmetric multiprocessor (SMP). Simple to program, but the shared path becomes the bottleneck.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)** — each processor has fast local memory and slower access to other processors' memory. Scales much further, but performance now depends on data placement.
- **COMA (cache-only memory architecture)** — all local memory is treated as a huge cache, and data migrates to where it is used.

## Interconnection structures

How processors reach memories and each other decides cost, bandwidth and scalability. Five structures appear in this syllabus.

**Time-shared common bus.** One bus; one transfer at a time. Cheapest and simplest, and easy to extend by plugging in another board, but the bus saturates quickly — practical limits are a handful of processors unless each has a large private cache to keep traffic off the bus. A **dual-bus** arrangement gives each processor a local bus to its own memory and I/O plus a shared system bus.

**Multiport memory.** Each memory module has several independent ports, one per processor, with fixed priority resolving simultaneous requests to the same module. Very high bandwidth and no bus arbitration delay, but the memory modules become complicated and expensive, and the number of processors is fixed at design time by the number of ports.

**Crossbar switch.** A grid with a crosspoint switch at every processor-memory intersection. All $n$ processors can access $n$ *different* memory modules simultaneously — maximum bandwidth of any structure. The cost is the problem: an $n \times m$ crossbar needs $n \times m$ crosspoints, growing quadratically, so a 64-way crossbar needs 4096 switches.

**Multistage interconnection network (MIN).** The compromise between the bus and the crossbar. Small $2\times2$ switches are arranged in stages, each switch able to pass straight through or cross over. An **omega network** connecting $n$ inputs to $n$ outputs uses

$$\log_2 n \text{ stages} \times \frac{n}{2} \text{ switches per stage} = \frac{n}{2}\log_2 n \text{ switches}$$

so $n=8$ needs $3 \times 4 = 12$ switches against the crossbar's 64, and $n=64$ needs 192 against 4096. Routing is done by the destination address: at stage $i$ the switch uses bit $i$ of the destination, sending the message up for 0 and down for 1. The cost of the saving is **blocking** — some permutations of source-to-destination pairs cannot be realised simultaneously, whereas a crossbar is non-blocking.

**Hypercube.** $2^d$ nodes, each labelled with a $d$-bit binary number and connected to the $d$ nodes whose labels differ in exactly one bit. Consequences that are asked numerically: **degree** $= d$ links per node, **diameter** $= d$ (the maximum number of hops is the maximum Hamming distance), and **total links** $= d\cdot 2^{d-1}$. A 16-node hypercube ($d = 4$) therefore has 4 links per node, diameter 4 and 32 links. Routing is beautifully simple: XOR the source and destination labels and fix the differing bits one at a time.

blocks.title: Worked example — sizing three interconnection networks
blocks.text:
Connect **64 processors** to **64 memory modules**.

**Crossbar.** Crosspoints $= 64 \times 64 = \mathbf{4096}$. Every processor can reach a distinct module at once: non-blocking, bandwidth 64 simultaneous transfers.

**Omega network.** Stages $= \log_2 64 = 6$; switches per stage $= 64/2 = 32$; total $= 6 \times 32 = \mathbf{192}$ switches of size $2\times2$. That is 4.7% of the crossbar's switch count, but the network blocks on some permutations and every message crosses 6 switches, adding latency.

**Single shared bus.** **1** shared path. Bandwidth is one transfer at a time, so with 64 processors each would get $1/64$ of the bus — useless without caches.

**Hypercube of the same 64 nodes.** $d = \log_2 64 = 6$. Each node has **6** links, the diameter is **6** hops, and the total number of links is $6 \times 2^{5} = 6\times32 = \mathbf{192}$ — coincidentally the same count as the omega network's switches, though they are different components.

**Routing in the hypercube.** From node 13 ($001101_2$) to node 42 ($101010_2$): XOR gives $100111_2$, so four bits differ and the path is four hops, correcting one differing bit per hop, for example $001101 \to 001100 \to 001110 \to 001010 \to 101010$. The route length always equals the Hamming distance, which is at most $d$.

blocks.q: An $8 \times 8$ omega network is built from $2\times2$ switches. How many switches does it contain, and is it blocking?
blocks.exp: Stages $= \log_2 8 = 3$ and each stage holds $8/2 = 4$ switches, so $3\times4 = \mathbf{12}$ switches. An omega network provides exactly one path between each input and output, so two connections needing the same intermediate link conflict: it is **blocking**. The 64 figure is the crossbar, which is non-blocking.

blocks.text:
## Interprocessor arbitration

Only one device may drive a shared bus at a time, so a **bus arbiter** grants mastership. The schemes mirror the priority-interrupt schemes of Unit 2.9.

**Serial (daisy-chain) arbitration.** A single bus-grant line is passed from one processor to the next in physical order. A processor that wants the bus and receives the grant takes it and blocks the grant from passing further; otherwise it passes it on. Cheap — one line regardless of the number of processors — but priority is fixed by position, the grant ripples (so delay grows with the number of processors), and a failed unit breaks the chain.

**Parallel arbitration.** Each processor has its own bus-request and bus-grant line into a central arbiter containing a priority encoder. Resolution is constant-time and priority can be changed, but the arbiter needs $2n$ lines for $n$ processors.

**Dynamic arbitration.** Priority is recomputed rather than fixed, so that no processor starves:

- **Rotating daisy chain** — the grant line is a ring and the starting point rotates, so the processor that last used the bus becomes lowest priority.
- **Round robin** — equal shares in a fixed rotation.
- **FIFO** — requests are queued and served in arrival order.
- **LRU** — highest priority goes to the processor that has waited longest.

## Interprocessor synchronisation

Shared memory means shared data structures, which means **mutual exclusion**. A software lock built from ordinary loads and stores is not safe on a multiprocessor, because two processors can both read a free lock before either writes it. Hardware must supply an **atomic read-modify-write** primitive, executed as one indivisible bus transaction:

- **Test-and-set (TSL)** — read a memory word into a register and set it to 1 in the same atomic operation. A processor spins until it reads 0, meaning it acquired the lock.
- **Swap / exchange** — atomically exchange a register with a memory word.
- **Compare-and-swap (CAS)** — write a new value only if the current value matches an expected one; the basis of most lock-free algorithms.
- **Fetch-and-add** — atomically add and return the old value; useful for counters and ticket locks.

Higher-level constructs — semaphores, monitors, barriers — are built on these. A **barrier** makes every processor wait until all have arrived, which is how phases of a parallel loop are separated.

A practical issue worth knowing: naive spinning on test-and-set generates a write (and therefore a coherence transaction) on every attempt, saturating the bus. The standard fix is **test-and-test-and-set** — spin on an ordinary read, which hits in the local cache, and attempt the atomic operation only when the read shows the lock free.

## Cache coherence

Give each processor a private cache and a correctness problem appears immediately. Suppose processors $P_1$ and $P_2$ both cache the variable $X = 5$. $P_1$ writes $X = 7$. With a **write-back** cache, main memory still holds 5 and $P_2$'s cache still holds 5, so three different values of one variable now exist. Even with **write-through**, memory is updated but $P_2$'s cached copy is stale. DMA makes the same problem appear on a uniprocessor: a device writing into memory invalidates cached copies without the cache knowing.

A system is **coherent** if a read returns the value of the most recent write to that location, and writes to the same location are seen in the same order by all processors.

**Snooping protocols** work on a broadcast medium such as a bus. Every cache controller watches all bus transactions and reacts to those touching blocks it holds.

- **Write-invalidate** — before writing, a processor broadcasts an invalidation; all other copies are marked invalid, so the writer holds the only copy and subsequent writes are local and free. This is what almost every real system uses.
- **Write-update (write-broadcast)** — every write is broadcast and all copies are updated. Readers never miss, but the bus traffic is proportional to writes rather than to sharing, which is usually much worse.

The standard write-invalidate protocol is **MESI**, in which every cache line is in one of four states:

| State | Meaning | Memory up to date? | Other copies? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M** odified | this cache has written it | no — this cache must write back | no |
| **E** xclusive | clean and uniquely held | yes | no |
| **S** hared | clean, possibly held elsewhere | yes | maybe |
| **I** nvalid | not usable | — | — |

The E state is the reason MESI beats the simpler three-state MSI: a line loaded by a single processor enters E, and a later write can move E $\to$ M **silently**, with no bus transaction at all. Without E, the first write to a privately used line would needlessly broadcast an invalidation. Extensions add **O** (owned, for cache-to-cache supply of dirty data) giving MOESI.

**Directory-based protocols** replace broadcasting with bookkeeping: a directory, distributed with the memory, records for each block which caches hold it and in what state. A write consults the directory and sends invalidations **point to point** only to the caches that actually have a copy. This costs directory storage (roughly one presence bit per cache per block) and an extra network round trip, but it scales to hundreds of processors where snooping cannot, because it needs no broadcast medium.

A third approach, used in simple systems, is **software coherence**: mark shared writable pages as non-cacheable, or flush caches at synchronisation points.

blocks.q: In the MESI protocol, a cache line is in the Exclusive state and the owning processor writes to it. What happens?
opts: The line moves to Modified and an invalidation is broadcast on the bus
The line moves to Modified with no bus transaction
The line moves to Shared and memory is updated
The line is invalidated and re-fetched from memory
blocks.exp: Exclusive already guarantees that no other cache holds the block, so nobody needs to be told. The write simply changes the state to Modified locally and is completed with **no bus traffic** — this silent E$\to$M upgrade is precisely what the E state was added for, and it is why MESI outperforms the three-state MSI protocol on privately used data.

blocks.text:
## Multicore processors

A **multicore** chip places several complete processors on one die, sharing the last-level cache, the memory controller and the pin interface. The shift happened because uniprocessor clock speed hit a power wall — dynamic power grows roughly with $C V^2 f$, and voltage could no longer be scaled down — so adding cores became the only way to convert transistors into performance.

Typical organisation: private L1 (and often L2) per core, a shared L3 on chip, coherence maintained by snooping over an on-chip ring or mesh, and a shared integrated memory controller. **Simultaneous multithreading (SMT / hyperthreading)** goes further by letting one core interleave instructions from several threads in the same cycle, filling issue slots that a single thread would leave empty; it adds throughput cheaply but does not double performance, since the threads contend for the same functional units and caches.

The hard limit on all of this is **Amdahl's law**. If a fraction $f$ of a program can be parallelised,

$$S(p) = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/p}, \qquad \lim_{p\to\infty}S = \frac{1}{1-f}$$

With $f = 0.90$ and $p = 8$, $S = 1/(0.1 + 0.1125) = 4.71$ — not 8. With $p = 100$, $S = 9.17$, still short of the ceiling of 10. Doubling the core count from 8 to 100 bought less than a factor of two, and that diminishing return, not transistor count, is what limits core counts in general-purpose machines. **Gustafson's law** offers the optimistic counterpart: if the problem *size* grows with the machine, the serial fraction shrinks and scaled speedup can stay near linear.

blocks.title: Worked example — Amdahl's law and the cost of the serial part
blocks.text:
A program spends 25% of its time in a strictly serial section and 75% in a section that parallelises perfectly.

**With 4 processors.**
$$S = \frac{1}{0.25 + 0.75/4} = \frac{1}{0.25 + 0.1875} = \frac{1}{0.4375} = \mathbf{2.29}$$

Efficiency $= S/p = 2.29/4 = 57\%$.

**With 16 processors.**
$$S = \frac{1}{0.25 + 0.75/16} = \frac{1}{0.25 + 0.046875} = \frac{1}{0.296875} = \mathbf{3.37}$$

Efficiency has collapsed to $3.37/16 = 21\%$: quadrupling the hardware bought a 47% gain.

**Ceiling.** $1/(1-f) = 1/0.25 = \mathbf{4}$. No amount of hardware can beat $4\times$.

**How much must the serial fraction shrink to reach a speedup of 8 with 16 processors?** Solve $8 = 1/[(1-f) + f/16]$:

$$0.125 = (1-f) + \frac{f}{16} = 1 - \frac{15f}{16} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{15f}{16} = 0.875 \;\Rightarrow\; f = \frac{14}{15} = 0.9333$$

So the parallel fraction must rise from 75% to **93.3%** — reducing the serial section from a quarter of the runtime to a fifteenth. That is the real message of Amdahl's law: optimising the serial part pays far more than adding processors.

tricks.title: Crossbar $n\times m$, omega $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$
tricks.body: Crosspoints grow quadratically, multistage switches grow as $n\log n$. For $n=64$ that is 4096 against 192. Quote the trade-off as 'crossbar is non-blocking and expensive, omega is blocking and cheap' and most comparison questions answer themselves.

tricks.title: Hypercube: degree = diameter = $d$, links = $d\,2^{d-1}$
tricks.body: All three follow from $2^d$ nodes labelled with $d$-bit strings. Routing distance between two nodes is the Hamming distance of their labels, so the worst case is $d$ hops and the average is $d/2$.

tricks.title: Amdahl backwards is often the real question
tricks.body: Given a target speedup $S$ on $p$ processors, solve $1/S = (1-f) + f/p$ for $f$. Rearranged, $f = \dfrac{1 - 1/S}{1 - 1/p}$. This answers 'what fraction must be parallelised' in one line.

tricks.title: MESI: E exists to make the first write free
tricks.body: If a question asks why MESI is better than MSI, or what happens on a write to an Exclusive line, the answer is the silent E$\to$M transition with no bus transaction. Every other state transition in MESI does generate bus traffic.

tricks.title: Snooping needs a broadcast medium, directories do not
tricks.body: That single structural fact decides which protocol a described system can use. A bus or ring implies snooping; a scalable point-to-point network with hundreds of nodes implies a directory.

traps.title: Write-through does not solve cache coherence
traps.body: It keeps main memory current but says nothing about the other processors' caches, which still hold stale copies. Coherence needs invalidation or update messages regardless of the write policy — a very common multiple-choice trap.

traps.title: Omega networks block; crossbars do not
traps.body: A multistage network offers exactly one path per input-output pair, so two connections sharing an internal link conflict even though their endpoints are distinct. Calling an omega network non-blocking is wrong, and so is calling a crossbar cheap.

traps.title: Tightly coupled means shared memory, not physical proximity
traps.body: The classification is about the communication mechanism: shared address space versus message passing. Two processors in the same rack connected only by a network are loosely coupled; two on separate boards sharing a memory bus are tightly coupled.

traps.title: Amdahl's speedup is never $p$, and efficiency falls fast
traps.body: With any non-zero serial fraction the speedup is bounded by $1/(1-f)$ regardless of $p$. Questions that appear to give a linear speedup are either assuming $f = 1$ or are really asking about Gustafson's scaled-speedup model.
